description_full: Deere & Company manufactures and distributes various equipment worldwide. It operates through four segments: Production and Precision Agriculture, Small Agriculture and Turf, Construction and Forestry, and Financial Services. The Production and Precision Agriculture segment provides track and row crop tractors, harvesters, cotton pickers and strippers, sugarcane harvesters and loaders, soil preparation, tillage, seeding, and crop care equipment; and application equipment, such as sprayers and nutrient management, soil preparation machinery, and related attachments and service parts. The Small Agriculture and Turf segment offers specialty, utility, and compact tractors; self-propelled forage harvesters and attachments; rotary mowers, hay and forage equipment, and utility vehicles; turf and utility equipment, including riding lawn, commercial mowing, and golf course equipment, and utility vehicles, as well as implements for mowing, tilling, snow and debris handling, aerating, residential, commercial, golf, and sports turf care applications. The Construction and Forestry segment provides backhoe loaders, crawler dozers and loaders, loaders, excavators, motor graders, articulated dump trucks, skid-steer loaders, milling machines, recyclers, slipform and asphalt pavers, surface miners, compactors, tandem, static rollers, mobile crushers and screens, mobile and stationary asphalt plants, and log harvesters; and road building and rehabilitation equipment. The Financial Services segment finances sales and leases agriculture and turf, and construction and forestry equipment. It also offers wholesale financing to dealers of the foregoing equipment; and extended equipment warranties. It has a strategic partnership with Tarter USA to develop and produce flex wing rotary cutters. It also has strategic partnership with Yamaha Motor Corporation, Usa to co-develop future side-by-side vehicles. The company was founded in 1837 and is headquartered in Moline, Illinois.

financial_summary: Deere & Company is a large-cap industrials business with a $181.1B market cap on $45.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -5% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 45% against a 9% cost of capital — a 36-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $6.1B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 3.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 21% operating margin runs 12pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.87x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.2% of sector revenue and 2.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 45% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.24 vs 5y 0.79), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $766.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 34% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $573 (margin of safety -17%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 55%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $439 to $764 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 37.3 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 27.5 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 29.7 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 77% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $694 on average, 3% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 45% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 36pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.86).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.48x.
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.1x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 5.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.6% over 3 years, 5.2% over 5 years and 4.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -1.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 4% of annual revenue.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (3.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 84%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (26 sales, net $50.4M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (0.6% in buybacks and 1.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 53 consecutive years, raising it 12.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 73,100 employees, each generates about $625K of revenue, 1.7x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.4% a year.
That works out to $83K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.3M (13x revenue per employee).
